name: Zoe Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the grid-connection crew, which means we build the new lines that hook solar farms and wind turbines up to the network. Most days I'm out in a field somewhere, setting poles with the digger-derrick, which is a truck that drills the hole and lifts the pole in one go. I love that what we build didn't exist last month. What wears me out is mud, and waiting on permits that sit in someone's inbox for weeks.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Nadia, who's a nurse on a surgical ward, in a little rented terrace in a market town. We've got about four months saved, and we're trying to get to a deposit. I use AI pretty much every day, for reading equipment specs, writing up my job sheets and quizzing myself for the evening diploma I'm doing in power engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly. I'd post something like, turns out the robots aren't coming, so let's get back to building the grid we actually need. On the crew I'd tease the older lads who were sure it was the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's solid. Every new solar farm needs a line, and there's a queue of them waiting to connect. My plan stays the same: finish the diploma and move up into design or project work over the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the diploma, two evenings a week, and finish it by 2028. I'd keep using AI for the boring bits, the job sheets and spec checks, because even small time savings add up. And Nadia and I would keep putting three hundred a month towards a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit disappointed. I like new things, so a world where nothing much changes is a little dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if AI stayed this small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time savings on paperwork, mostly. Right now AI turns my scribbled notes into a proper job sheet in two minutes. If that's all it ever does, I'd still use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at home a worry, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, a bit. Every time we get closer to a deposit, prices move. But Nadia's job is safe and so is mine, so I'm not losing sleep. It's more frustration than worry.

think: Her job is **solid**, since every new solar farm needs a line.
The plan stays: finish the **diploma** and move into design work.
do: Finish the **power engineering diploma** by 2028, two evenings a week.
Keep using AI for **job sheets** and spec checks.
Save **three hundred a month** towards a house deposit with Nadia.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of disappointment at a dull, unchanging world.

fieldNote: Her security comes from the **renewables build-out** and her partner's stable job.

House prices are a **frustration**, not a real fear.

steps.text: Finish the power engineering diploma by 2028
Keep using AI to write job sheets and check specs
Save three hundred a month towards a deposit with Nadia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for building things, as long as workers get a say. Online I'd push the line that unions should be bargaining for training in these tools right now, not fighting them. I'd probably share my own tricks with the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out ahead. The hands-on side of my job stays, and I'm already good with the tools. If design and planning get faster, there are more projects, and someone who can climb and read a plan is useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to put me on the AI planning trial if there is one, the first month it's offered. I'd switch my diploma project to how AI can speed up connection design. And I'd run a lunchtime session for the crew showing them the job-sheet trick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It feels like a door opening for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned permits sitting in inboxes. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, hugely. If software checks the plans and books the outage windows, a solar farm connection that takes eight months might take four. That's more solar farms on the grid and more work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, our crew lead, for one. He's brilliant on a pole, but he hates screens, and if all the paperwork moves onto a tablet he'll struggle. I'd want to help him, not watch him get pushed out.

think: She'll **come out ahead**, keeping hands-on work and good tool skills.

Switch her diploma project to **AI connection design**.
Run a **lunchtime session** teaching the crew her job-sheet method.

steps.text: Volunteer for the AI planning trial the first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the robots should belong to all of us, not just to a few companies. If an AI can design a grid connection and a robot can build it, then power should get cheaper and workers should share the gains. I'd join any campaign pushing for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my diploma suddenly looks half useless, because the design work I was aiming for goes first, in 2028. The climbing lasts until about 2031. So I'd have three years where I'm the person who knows both, and then I need to be the person who runs the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the diploma and move straight into whatever robotics or drone course the company or college runs. I'd ask to be on the first robot crew trials, as a lead or tester. And Nadia and I would pause the house hunt and keep the deposit money as a cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an active kind of anxious. My brain starts planning straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots around 2031. What do those three years mean for someone who does both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. The three years before the robots are the window to become the robot lead rather than the person the robot replaces. If I waste them, I'm thirty-one with a trade that's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia would say her ward will still need people, and she's probably right for a while. We'd talk about her being the steady one while I take the risks. She's always been the sensible one, honestly.

Workers should **share the gains** if AI and robots build the grid.

She switches course fast, typical of her **adaptability**.
Nadia's **steady nursing job** lets her take risks.

steps.text: Switch from the diploma to a robotics or drone course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, really, but with more time to organise. I'd say let's use these five years to write the rules: public ownership, training for every lineworker, and a share of the savings. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to get ready properly. I'd be thirty-four when robots take over hands-on work. If I spend the first few years mastering the AI design tools and the robot crews, I'm in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to fund a robotics course alongside my day job. I'd start testing AI design tools on small projects to see what they get wrong. And Nadia and I would keep saving and maybe buy a smaller place, so the mortgage is easy whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anxious. It's a big change, but it's one I can see coming and plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years to see it coming, what do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd finish it by 2028, but I'd lean the final project hard into AI design. Knowing how the grid system should work is what lets you catch the AI when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you finish the diploma in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev again, honestly. Five years is enough for him to retire comfortably. For the younger lads who don't like screens, it's harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can get it right. A decade is enough to train everybody and plan the grid properly. I'd push the union to make a ten-year plan and hold the company to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty calm about this one. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes. By then I could be a design engineer who also knows the field, and ready to run robot crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma, then go for a full engineering degree part-time, maybe paid by the company. We'd buy the house we want now, since there's time. And I'd keep using AI daily, so I'm fluent by the time it really matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited. It's long enough to feel like an adventure, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. How does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I don't have to drop anything. I can finish my diploma, do the degree and still be early on the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2039 I'd be running a robot connection crew out of a van, with a laptop and a big flask of coffee. Probably training apprentices on what the robots can't see.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole plan would have to change overnight. What would help is fast, paid training, like a robotics course I can do while still earning, and a union that's already negotiating about robots instead of waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the robots. That's the question nobody asks at work. If the electricity company owns the robots, fine, but then the savings should come back to the people who pay the bills.

headlineQuote: If the electricity company owns the robots, fine, but then the savings should come back to the people who pay the bills.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old lineworker on a **grid-connection crew** building lines to solar and wind farms.
She lives with **Nadia**, a nurse, and they save towards a house deposit.
She uses AI daily and is studying for a **power engineering diploma**.
She welcomes slow change and sees AGI by 2028 as **upending her plan**.
With time she'd **run robot crews**, and wants their savings shared publicly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her design career plan would fall apart overnight.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid robotics training** while earning, and a union already bargaining on robots.
